editorial.body.old_excerpt: **This KBLI activity is deliberately narrow: it covers the making of tempe from soybeans.*
editorial.body.new:
**This KBLI activity is deliberately narrow: it covers the making of tempe from soybeans.** The record does not frame it as a broad fermented-food category, a general protein-manufacturing activity, or a catch-all for every product called tempe. Its scope is the production activity itself, anchored in one raw material: kedelai, or soybeans. That precision matters because the commercial identity of the product may feel familiar, even domestic, but the registration question is still technical. The code is about what is being made, from what input, and under which registered industrial activity.

For operators, the scale picture is unusually straightforward. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses. In practical registration language, that means the activity is not reserved only for cottage producers or only for large industry; it can sit across the full scale ladder recorded here. A founder setting up a small production unit, a growing local processor, or a larger manufacturing operation would all read the same scale field before moving on to the ownership and location question.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II: soybean tempe manufacturing is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (p.2, entry 4, sub-row "Industri tempe kedelai", ex-KBLI 2020 10391). A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for tempe making is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. Bali's provincial overlay does not change that answer: the record lists 10307 outside the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026, but the national reservation already decides the PMA question.

This KBLI activity is for making woven goods whose main material is rattan or bamboo. The record’s scope is practical and material-led: mats, webbing, lampit, hand fans, woven wall panels, and woven bags, including women’s bags and laptop bags. Its centre of gravity is not general craft trading or a broad lifestyle label; it is manufacturing, where the defining feature is the woven article and the principal input is rattan or bamboo.

That makes the registration question more specific than it first appears. The code is available across the full range of business scales listed in the record: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. A small workshop producing hand fans and woven panels, a growing bag producer, and a larger woven-goods manufacturer can all sit inside the same activity description if the actual production remains within the stated scope. The record also draws a boundary away from footwear and woven headwear, so the clean reading is to keep this code for rattan-and-bamboo woven goods themselves, not every product that happens to use a woven element.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II: rattan and bamboo weaving is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (p.4, entry 14 "Industri barang anyaman", sub-row "Rotan dan bambu", KBLI 16291). A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for rattan and bamboo weaving is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. That is not a Bali percentage cap and not a negotiable limit; it is a national reservation. Bali's provincial overlay does not change that answer: the record lists 16291 outside the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026, but the national reservation already decides the PMA question.

KBLI 16293 is a manufacturing activity for wooden craft and carved objects that are not furniture. The record describes the activity through its products: reliefs, masks, statues, wayang, flower vases, frames, lampshades, souvenirs, ashtrays, tissue boxes, jewelry boxes, wall-decoration products, and name boards. That matters because this code is not limited to one size of enterprise in the national classification record. A founder reading the scope should therefore focus less on the aesthetic style of the goods and more on whether the business is actually producing the listed kinds of wooden craft or carving products.

A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for wood carving is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. editorial.body.old_excerpt: KBLI 32201 is about craft, sound, and cultural manufacture rather than performance or reta
editorial.body.new:
KBLI 32201 is about craft, sound, and cultural manufacture rather than performance or retail. The record defines it as the making of traditional musical instruments with roots in Indonesian cultural history or customary practice. These are instruments played by plucking, bowing, blowing, or striking: angklung, calung, kecapi, bamboo flute, kolintang, gong, traditional trumpet, gambang, rebab, and tifa are all within the recorded scope. The same record also brings in whistles, call horns, and other blown sound-signalling instruments, so the code is not limited to ceremonial instruments alone. Its centre of gravity, however, is clear: physical production of traditional sound-making objects.

The registration picture is broad at the national scale. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar businesses, meaning the record does not reserve this manufacturing activity for only one size of operator. A small workshop making bamboo flutes and a larger facility producing gongs or other traditional instruments would both sit inside the scale range named in the record, as long as the activity remains the making of the instruments covered by the scope.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II: the making of traditional musical instruments is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM (p.6, entry 23 "Industri alat musik tradisional antara lain: Angklung, Gordang Sembilan, Dambus, Kolintang, Gendang Beleq, Sasando, Tifa", KBLI 32201 — the list is by example, not a restriction). A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for instrument making is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia. No separate Bali percentage applies and none should be read into it. Bali's provincial overlay does not change that answer: the record lists 32201 outside the 18 business fields Bali closed to new PMA licensing in 2026, but the national reservation already decides the PMA question.

editorial.body.old_excerpt: KBLI 55106 is the commercial provision of non-star hotel accommodation, ordinarily offered
editorial.body.new:
KBLI 55106 is the commercial provision of non-star hotel accommodation, ordinarily offered on a daily or weekly basis. It applies where an operator manages all or part of a building that meets the requirements for a non-star hotel. The scope expressly accommodates both building-area bands: premises above 6,000 m² and premises at or below 6,000 m². The point is not a particular style of hospitality, but commercially managed short-stay accommodation within that non-star hotel framework.

The activity is open to small, medium and large businesses. That matters because the code does not reserve the field for a single operating scale: a modest accommodation business and a larger hotel operation can each sit within the stated scope, provided the actual activity fits it.

The ownership position is set by Perpres 10/2021, as amended by Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran II (p.15, entry 48, sub-row "Hotel Melati", ex-KBLI 2020 55120): non-star hotel operation is allocated to Koperasi and UMKM. A foreign investor can be neither a cooperative nor a UMKM, so the national foreign-ownership ceiling recorded for non-star hotels is 0% and a PT PMA cannot register this code anywhere in Indonesia.

Bali adds a second, independent closure: the provincial government lists the non-star hotel among the 18 business fields it closed to new foreign-owned licensing on OSS from May 2026. For a founder the conclusion is precise rather than scope-dependent: this is not a question to be resolved by the declared scope in OSS; the code is not available to a foreign-owned company at either level.
